# What command-line mode is

The `mitopilot` command runs a project from raw reads to GenBank files without
opening the app or an R console. It is made for people who are comfortable in a
shell, and for anyone who wants to run many samples overnight on a cluster.

The idea is simple. MitoPilot runs every step. A sample that passes a set of
checks moves on by itself. A sample that fails a check is **parked** with a
reason, and a person looks at it. Nothing is hidden: every parked sample, every
override, and every dropped sample is recorded in the project.

The app and the command line share one project. You can start a project in the
shell, open it in the app to fix a parked sample, then go back to the shell. You
can also do it the other way round.

<div class="alert alert-note">
<strong>Note.</strong> Editing settings from the terminal and a guided review
walk-through are planned but not here yet. Until then, change settings and
review parked samples in the app, as usual.
</div>

# Getting the `mitopilot` command

## Container-based install

Run this once, from an R session that has MitoPilot installed:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
Rscript -e 'MitoPilot::install_cli()'
```

This writes a small `mitopilot` command to `~/.local/bin`. If that folder is not
on your `PATH`, the command prints the line to add to your shell startup file:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Check that it works:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot --help
```

## Native install (no containers)

Source the environment first, then install the command with the Rscript from
that environment:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
source <install_dir>/activate.sh
Rscript -e 'MitoPilot::install_cli()'
```

In later sessions, `source <install_dir>/activate.sh` is all you need if
`~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`. See
[Installing without containers](Native-Install.html).

# Quick start

MitoPilot ships three small test projects. Pick one and run it from start to
finish:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot init my_test --test reads        # or: assemblies, annotations
cd my_test
mitopilot auto
mitopilot status
```

- `--test reads` starts from raw reads, so MitoPilot assembles and annotates.
- `--test assemblies` starts from finished assemblies, so it annotates only.
- `--test annotations` starts from finished annotations.

`auto` can take a while on a laptop. Use `mitopilot auto --dry-run` to see what
it would do without running anything.

# How `auto` works

`mitopilot auto` does the whole job in order:

1. Runs the assemble pipeline for every sample that is waiting.
2. Accepts each assembly that passes the pass rules. The others are parked.
3. Runs the annotate pipeline for the accepted assemblies.
4. Accepts each annotation that passes the pass rules. The others are parked.
5. Puts accepted samples into an export group. The group is named after the
   project folder; use `--group NAME` to choose another name.
6. Runs the outlier check on each group and exports GenBank files. Samples
   flagged by the check are handled as `--flagged` says (see below).
7. Prints a summary: how many were accepted, how many are parked, and how many
   groups were exported or held back.

It is safe to run `auto` again at any time. It picks up where it stopped, skips
finished work, and leaves alone any sample you put on hold. After you fix a
parked sample, run `mitopilot auto` again to carry it on.

Useful options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--group NAME` | Name of the export group (default: the project folder name) |
| `--flagged stop\|drop\|keep` | What to do with samples flagged at export (default: `stop`) |
| `--no-resume` | Start the pipelines fresh instead of resuming |
| `--submit` | Send the whole job to the cluster scheduler instead of running it here |
| `--dry-run` | Show what would run, then stop |
| `--yes` | Answer yes to every confirmation |
| `--project DIR` | Use a project other than the current folder |

# The pass rules

A sample passes only if none of the rules below fire. When a rule fires, its
code is shown in the `reasons` column of `mitopilot status`.

| Stage | Reason code | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Assemble | `not_run` | The assembly step has not run yet. |
| Assemble | `failed` | The assembly step ran and failed. |
| Assemble | `multiple_paths` | The assembler found more than one possible path; a person must choose. |
| Assemble | `multiple_scaffolds` | The assembly has more than one scaffold. |
| Assemble | `linear` | The assembly is not circular (unless you allow linear assemblies). |
| Assemble | `low_coverage` | Mean read depth is below the minimum. |
| Assemble | `poor_reference` | The closest reference found by BLAST is poor or missing. |
| Annotate | `not_run` | The annotate step has not run yet. |
| Annotate | `failed` | The annotate step ran and failed. |
| Annotate | `warnings` | Curation and validation left one or more warnings, or the count is missing. |
| Annotate | `problematic` | The annotation is marked as problematic. |
| Either | `output_missing` | An expected output file is missing, so the sample cannot be accepted. |
| Annotate | `assembly_not_accepted` | The assembly behind this annotation was not accepted. |
| Export | `start_offset`, `stop_offset`, `low_identity`, `internal_stop` | Outlier check flags: a gene starts or stops far from its neighbours, matches the group poorly, or has a stop codon inside. |

Two switches change the rules. Both are set with `mitopilot rules`:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot rules                              # show the current values
mitopilot rules --min-coverage 20            # raise the minimum mean depth (default 10)
mitopilot rules --accept-linear              # let linear assemblies pass
mitopilot rules --no-accept-linear           # go back to requiring circular ones
```

# Reading `status`

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot status
mitopilot status --parked
mitopilot status --stage annotate
mitopilot status --json
```

`status` prints one row per sample, or per annotation unit when a sample has
more than one. The columns show the stage, whether the sample is accepted
(locked), who accepted it, the reason codes of any parked sample, and its export
group. A line at the end counts the units, and a second line tallies warnings
across the project.

- `--parked` shows only the samples waiting for a decision.
- `--stage` limits the table to `assemble`, `annotate`, or `export`.
- `--json` prints machine-readable output for scripts.

# Dealing with parked samples

For anything that needs eyes, such as picking between assembly paths or fixing
a gene boundary, open the project in the app as usual. Everything you do there
is picked up by the next `mitopilot auto`.

For the rest, three commands cover it. Name samples by ID, or as
`ID:path:scaffold` to pick one annotation unit of a sample that has several.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot accept S01 S02 --override --reason "checked in the app, fine"
mitopilot accept --all-parked --override --reason "reviewed all"
mitopilot hold S03
mitopilot requeue S04
```

- `accept` moves a sample on. Without `--override` it only accepts samples that
  already pass the rules. With `--override` it accepts samples that fail, and
  `--reason` records why.
- `hold` stops a sample from being queued until you decide.
- `requeue` sends a sample back to run again, for example after you changed its
  settings in the app.

Every override is written to a review log in the project, with the rules that
failed, your reason, and the time. Nothing is accepted past the rules silently.

# Grouping and export

Accepted samples are put into export groups. `auto` does this for you. To do it
by hand:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot group batch1 --all-accepted
mitopilot group batch1 --samples S01,S02,S03
mitopilot group batch1 --all-accepted --split
```

GenBank does not take complete and partial genomes in one submission, so a
group cannot hold both. If your samples are mixed, `--split` makes two groups,
`batch1-complete` and `batch1-partial`. `auto` always splits when it needs to.
A sample whose completeness is not known is left without a group.

Export one group with:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot export batch1 --flagged ask
```

Before writing files, MitoPilot runs the outlier check on the group and writes
an HTML alignment report next to the export. The `--flagged` option says what to
do with samples the check flags:

| Value | What happens |
|---|---|
| `ask` | Ask you in the terminal (the default when you are at a terminal). |
| `stop` | Export nothing and exit with status 2 (the default in scripts and in `auto`). |
| `drop` | Leave the flagged samples out and export the rest. |
| `keep` | Export everything, flagged samples included. This is logged as an override and needs confirmation (or `--yes`). |

The export uses the FASTA header template you last used in the app's export
window, and it says which template it picked. The thresholds and options from
that window are used too. Samples dropped at export are recorded in the review
log, so a later `auto` does not try to export them again. The alignment report
still shows dropped samples.

Fetch sample metadata from online sources before export if you use it:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot metadata fetch --source geome
```

# Running individual steps

`auto` is a loop over smaller commands. You can run the pieces yourself:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot run assemble
mitopilot run annotate --auto-accept
mitopilot run assemble --dry-run
```

- `--auto-accept` accepts the samples that pass the rules once the run ends.
- `--dry-run` shows what would run and stops.
- `--no-resume` starts the pipeline fresh instead of resuming.
- `--submit` sends the run to your cluster scheduler (see below).
- `--yes` skips confirmation questions.

`run` exits with status 2 when some samples of that stage are parked.

# Running on a cluster

If your project uses a scheduler such as Slurm, SGE, PBS, or LSF, set up a
cluster profile once, then check it before a real run.

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot cluster setup
mitopilot cluster list
mitopilot cluster show my_cluster
mitopilot cluster check my_cluster
```

`cluster setup` asks which scheduler you use, the queue, time, memory, account,
and any lines to run first (such as `module load` lines). It saves a cluster
profile and a job submit template, then offers to run the check.

`cluster check` tests four things in order and stops at the first failure. On a
busy queue add `--wait 900` to give the test job more time.

| Stage | What a pass means |
|---|---|
| `tools` | The scheduler commands, Nextflow, Java, and your container engine were found. |
| `config` | The cluster configuration file reads without errors. |
| `submit` | A small job ran on a compute node and found Nextflow, Java, and the `mitopilot` command there. |
| `pipeline` | MitoPilot started inside a real pipeline task on a compute node. |

A healthy check ends with `4 passed, 0 skipped`. A project that uses the local
executor shows `submit` as skipped, because there is no scheduler. If the test
job times out, MitoPilot cancels the job it submitted. Look at your queue
(`squeue`, `qstat`, or `bjobs`) to confirm that none is left.

<div class="alert alert-note">
<strong>LSF sites.</strong> MitoPilot submits with <code>bsub script</code>. Some
LSF versions only read the <code>#BSUB</code> lines when the script comes in on
standard input. If the check job runs with default resources, that is the
cause. Edit the submit template (below) or ask your cluster staff.
</div>

Use a saved profile with a project:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot init my_proj --test reads --executor my_cluster
mitopilot cluster apply my_cluster --project my_proj
mitopilot cluster check --project my_proj
```

`apply` copies the profile's submit template into the project. An existing
project template is backed up first.

To change a profile later, open it in your editor (`$EDITOR`, then `$VISUAL`,
then `vi`):

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot cluster edit my_cluster            # the cluster configuration
mitopilot cluster edit my_cluster --submit   # the job submit template
```

Run any step on the cluster, instead of on the node where you typed it, with
`--submit`. Add `--dry-run` first to read the job script:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot run assemble --submit --dry-run
mitopilot auto --submit
```

If MitoPilot's built-in scheduler types do not fit your site, choose the closest
one in `cluster setup`, then open the submit template with
`mitopilot cluster edit NAME --submit` and change the header lines and the
setup lines to match your site. The template needs the two placeholders
`<<NEXTFLOW_CMD>>` and `<<LOG_FILE>>`; keep them where they are.
[HPC cluster support](Custom-HPC.html) explains the cluster configuration in
more detail.

# Using the command in scripts

Every command returns an exit status:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Done, nothing left to decide. |
| 1 | An error: bad input, a failed run, or a missing file. |
| 2 | Finished, but a person needs to look: parked samples, flagged samples, or nothing exported. |

A short example that branches on status 2:

```{bash eval=FALSE}
mitopilot auto --yes --project /data/my_project
status=$?
if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "All done"
elif [ "$status" -eq 2 ]; then
  echo "Some samples need review"
  mitopilot status --parked --project /data/my_project
else
  echo "Something went wrong" >&2
  exit 1
fi
```

Other points for scripts:

- `--yes` answers yes to every confirmation. Without a terminal, commands that
  would ask refuse to guess and tell you which choice to pass instead.
- `--project DIR` points a command at a project, so you do not need to `cd`
  into it. Without it, the current folder is the project.
- Only one pipeline run can be active in a project at a time.
- Press Ctrl-C to stop a running pipeline. It stops cleanly and writes a
  stopped run report, so the run appears in the app's Run Reports window. Run
  the same command again to resume.

Run Reports in the app mark runs started from the command line, so you can tell
them from runs started in the app.

# What is coming later

Two things are planned for a later release: editing project settings from the
terminal, and a guided walk-through for reviewing parked samples. Until then,
change settings and review parked samples in the app. The two ways of working
share the same project, so you can switch at any time.
